behaviorNotes: Works well in baking and sauces. Slightly sweeter than cow's milk. Use barista-style for frothing. May thin out cream-based sauces slightly.
limitations: Not suitable for recipes requiring high-fat dairy. Contains gluten (not safe for celiac).

behaviorNotes: Thinner than cow's milk. Works in baking but may produce a lighter texture. Unsweetened varieties are best for savory cooking.
limitations: Contains tree nuts. Not safe for nut allergy clients. Lower protein content than cow's milk.

behaviorNotes: Closest protein content to cow's milk. Curdles when mixed with acidic ingredients; add acid slowly. Good for baking, sauces, and custards.
limitations: Contains soy. Not safe for soy allergy clients. May impart a slightly beany flavor.

behaviorNotes: Rich and creamy. Imparts a coconut flavor. Full-fat canned coconut milk is best for sauces, curries, and soups. Coconut beverage (carton) is thinner.
cuisineContext: Best in curries, Thai/Indian cuisine, and tropical desserts
limitations: Strong coconut flavor may not suit all dishes. While coconut is technically a drupe, FDA classifies it as a tree nut for labeling purposes.

ratio: 7/8 cup oil per 1 cup butter
behaviorNotes: Baked goods will be more moist and dense. Loses the buttery flavor. Works for quick breads, muffins, and cakes. Not ideal for pie crust or pastry.
limitations: Does not work for laminated doughs (croissant, puff pastry). No browning/Maillard reaction from milk solids.

behaviorNotes: Closest behavior to real butter. Works in most applications including pastry. Miyoko's brand performs well in laminated doughs. Check ingredients for soy/nut content.
limitations: Some brands contain soy or coconut. Verify for nut/soy allergies. May have slightly different melting point than dairy butter.

ratio: 1/2 cup applesauce per 1 cup butter
behaviorNotes: Reduces fat content significantly. Keeps baked goods moist. Best when replacing only half the butter; replacing all butter yields a gummy texture.
limitations: Not for pastry, cookies that need structure, or savory cooking. Adds subtle fruit flavor.

behaviorNotes: Thick and rich. Whips similarly to heavy cream when chilled. Imparts coconut flavor. Refrigerate can overnight and use solid portion only for whipping.
limitations: Coconut flavor is pronounced. Not suitable for all savory sauces. FDA classifies coconut as tree nut.

targetIngredient: cashew cream (soaked cashews blended with water)
ratio: 1:1 (1 cup raw cashews + 3/4 cup water, blended until smooth)
behaviorNotes: Neutral flavor. Excellent in pasta sauces, soups, and cream-based dishes. Blends very smooth. Soak cashews 4+ hours or boil 15 minutes before blending.
limitations: Contains tree nuts. Not safe for nut allergy clients. Higher cost than dairy cream.

ratio: 2-3 tbsp nutritional yeast per 1/4 cup parmesan
behaviorNotes: Provides umami and cheesy flavor. Does not melt or behave like cheese. Best as a finishing ingredient or in sauces with a fat base.
limitations: No melting capability. Texture is powdery/flaky, not stretchy. Cannot replace cheese in pizza, quesadillas, or grilled cheese.

ratio: 1 tbsp ground flaxseed + 3 tbsp water per 1 egg (let sit 5 min to gel)
behaviorNotes: Provides binding but no leavening. Works best in dense baked goods (muffins, brownies, pancakes). Adds slight nutty flavor. Let the mixture gel 5 minutes before using.
limitations: Does not work for meringues, souffles, or recipes relying on egg for structure/lift. Adds a visible speckled appearance.

ratio: 1 tbsp chia seeds + 3 tbsp water per 1 egg (let sit 5 min to gel)
behaviorNotes: Similar to flax egg. Provides binding. Neutral flavor. Visible seed specks in final product. Let gel 5 minutes before using.
limitations: Same as flax egg. No leavening. Does not work for egg-forward dishes. Seeds are visible.

ratio: 3 tbsp aquafaba per 1 egg white; 2 tbsp per 1 egg yolk
behaviorNotes: Whips to stiff peaks like egg whites. Works for meringue, mousse, and macarons. Use liquid from unsalted canned chickpeas. Reduce by half on stovetop for stronger whip.
limitations: Contains legumes (chickpeas). Meringues may weep more than egg white versions. Flavor is neutral when whipped.

ratio: 1/4 cup (about half a banana) per 1 egg
behaviorNotes: Adds moisture and binding. Imparts banana flavor. Best in sweet baked goods where banana flavor is welcome.
limitations: Strong banana flavor. Not suitable for savory dishes or neutral-flavored baked goods. Adds sweetness.

targetIngredient: commercial egg replacer (Bob's Red Mill, JUST Egg)
ratio: Follow package directions (varies by brand)
behaviorNotes: JUST Egg (mung bean based) works for scrambles, omelets, and quiche. Powder replacers (Bob's Red Mill) work for baking. Best all-around egg replacement.
limitations: Check ingredients for allergens (some contain soy). Cost is higher than eggs. Availability varies by region.

ratio: 1:1 by volume (but add 1 extra egg or binding agent per cup)
behaviorNotes: High fat, no gluten. Baked goods are denser and moister. Browns faster due to fat content. Reduce oven temp by 25F. Works well in cookies, cakes, and crusts.
limitations: Contains tree nuts. No gluten structure means no bread, pizza dough, or pasta. Cannot be used for roux or thickening.

ratio: 7/8 cup rice flour per 1 cup wheat flour (add xanthan gum: 1/2 tsp per cup)
behaviorNotes: Finer texture than wheat flour. Gritty if not finely milled. Best combined with a starch (tapioca, potato) for better texture. Good for coating/frying.
limitations: No gluten structure. Baked goods are crumbly without xanthan gum or other binder. Not suitable alone for bread.

ratio: 1 1/3 cups oat flour per 1 cup wheat flour
behaviorNotes: Slightly sweet, nutty flavor. Absorbs more liquid than wheat flour. Use certified gluten-free oats for celiac clients. Can make at home by blending rolled oats.
limitations: Must use certified gluten-free oats for celiac. Dense in yeast breads. Not suitable for delicate pastries.

ratio: 1/4 cup coconut flour per 1 cup wheat flour (add 1 extra egg per 1/4 cup coconut flour)
behaviorNotes: Extremely absorbent. Requires significantly more liquid and eggs than wheat flour. Dense and dry if not adjusted properly. Always sift before using.
limitations: Cannot substitute 1:1. Requires recipe reformulation. Coconut flavor is noticeable. FDA classifies coconut as tree nut for labeling.

ratio: 2 tbsp tapioca starch per 1 tbsp cornstarch
behaviorNotes: Glossy finish, slightly chewy texture. Withstands freezing and reheating better than cornstarch. Good for fruit pies and stir-fry sauces.
limitations: Over-thickening creates a slimy texture. Breaks down with prolonged cooking. Use in the last few minutes.

behaviorNotes: Similar texture and richness. Slightly more earthy flavor. May turn green in baking due to chlorogenic acid reacting with baking soda (harmless). Add 1 tsp lemon juice to prevent.
limitations: Green discoloration in baked goods is cosmetic but may alarm clients. Contains seeds (safe for nut allergies unless seed allergy exists).

behaviorNotes: Closest flavor match to peanut butter. Good in sandwiches, sauces, and baking. Check labels for cross-contamination warnings.
limitations: Contains soy. Not safe for soy allergy clients. Cross-contamination with peanuts is possible depending on manufacturer.

behaviorNotes: Similar size and texture when toasted. Slightly different flavor (less sweet, more savory). Excellent in pesto, salads, and grain bowls.
limitations: Different flavor profile. Works well in savory applications but less so in desserts that rely on pine nut sweetness.

behaviorNotes: Good crunch substitute. Toast for best flavor. Works in salads, granola, and as a coating for proteins.
limitations: Different flavor. Less visually elegant as a garnish. May turn green in baked goods with baking soda.

behaviorNotes: Nut-free alternative to almond flour. Similar fat content and behavior. May turn green in baked goods with baking soda. Add 1 tsp lemon juice per cup to prevent.
limitations: Green discoloration in baked goods. Stronger flavor than almond flour. More expensive in some markets.

ratio: 1:1 by weight
behaviorNotes: Press tofu for 30 minutes to remove moisture. Pan-fry until golden before adding to curries for best texture. Absorbs flavors well in marinades.
limitations: Contains soy. Different texture (softer than paneer even when pressed). Does not have the same milky richness.

ratio: 1:1 by weight
behaviorNotes: Crumble and pan-fry with seasonings. Steam tempeh for 10 minutes before cooking to reduce bitterness. Takes on marinades and seasonings well. Nutty, fermented flavor.
limitations: Contains soy. Fermented flavor is distinct. Does not render fat like ground beef; add oil for browning.

ratio: Two 14oz cans per 1 lb pulled pork
behaviorNotes: Drain, shred with a fork, and cook with BBQ sauce. Texture is remarkably similar to pulled pork. Very little inherent flavor; absorbs seasonings completely.
limitations: No protein content (unlike pork). Must be young/green jackfruit (not ripe). Available canned; fresh is harder to find.

ratio: 1:1 by volume (or blend 50/50 with remaining meat for flexitarian option)
behaviorNotes: Rich umami flavor. Cook mushrooms until all moisture evaporates for best texture. Combines well with soy sauce and tomato paste for deeper savoriness.
limitations: Softer texture than meat. Releases a lot of moisture during cooking; cook dry before combining with other ingredients.

ratio: 1:1 (may need extra salt; coconut aminos is sweeter and less salty)
behaviorNotes: Sweeter and milder than soy sauce. Lower sodium. Made from coconut sap. Add a pinch of salt to match soy sauce saltiness. Soy-free and gluten-free.
cuisineContext: Asian cuisine, marinades, stir-fries, dipping sauces
limitations: Sweeter flavor profile. Higher cost than soy sauce. May need additional salt. FDA classifies coconut as tree nut for labeling.

behaviorNotes: Richer, less sharp flavor than regular soy sauce. Most tamari is gluten-free but always verify label says 'gluten-free'. Contains soy.
cuisineContext: Asian cuisine, marinades, all soy sauce applications
limitations: Still contains soy. Not suitable for soy allergy. Verify gluten-free certification for celiac clients.

ratio: 1:1 by weight
behaviorNotes: Cooks faster than wheat pasta. Gets mushy if overcooked; test 1-2 minutes before package time. Rinse after cooking to remove excess starch and prevent sticking.
limitations: Softer texture, breaks more easily. Does not hold shape as well in baked pasta dishes. Stickier than wheat pasta.

ratio: 1:1 by weight
behaviorNotes: Higher protein than wheat pasta. Earthier flavor. Holds shape better than rice pasta. Chickpea pasta is the most neutral tasting. Check for wheat cross-contamination on label.
limitations: Distinct legume flavor that not all clients enjoy. Edamame pasta contains soy. May foam during cooking.

behaviorNotes: Deep umami from dried shiitakes and kombu seaweed. Steep dried shiitakes and kombu in water overnight or simmer 30 minutes. Strain before using. Closest flavor profile to seafood stock.
limitations: Different flavor character. No brininess. Add a pinch of seaweed salt for ocean-like quality.

behaviorNotes: Brands like Fysh or homemade versions use dried shiitakes, soy sauce, and seaweed. Similar umami depth. May contain soy.
limitations: May contain soy. Flavor is close but distinguishable from fish sauce. Homemade version requires planning.

behaviorNotes: Widely available (Lee Kum Kee makes a vegetarian version). Similar sweetness and umami. May contain soy and wheat.
limitations: May contain soy, wheat, or MSG depending on brand. Verify ingredients for relevant allergies.

ratio: 1:1 by weight
behaviorNotes: More forgiving to cook (higher fat content prevents drying). More flavorful. Takes longer to cook than breast. Remove skin or leave on depending on application. Boneless thighs are most versatile.
limitations: Higher fat content. Darker color may not suit all presentations. Takes slightly longer to cook through.

targetIngredient: pork shoulder (cut into medallions or cubed)
ratio: 1:1 by weight
behaviorNotes: Much cheaper per pound. More marbling means more flavor. Requires different cooking method: braise, slow-roast, or stew. Cannot quick-sear like tenderloin.
limitations: Requires longer cooking time. Tougher if not cooked low-and-slow. Different texture and presentation than tenderloin.

ratio: 1 cup dried = about 3 cups cooked (one 15oz can)
behaviorNotes: About 50-70% cheaper. Better texture and flavor. Soak overnight or quick-soak (boil 1 min, rest 1 hour). Cook 1-2 hours depending on variety. Salt after cooking.
limitations: Requires planning ahead (overnight soak). Longer cook time. Uneven results if beans are old.

ratio: 1:1 by weight (do not thaw before adding to batter; add 1 tbsp extra flour to prevent bleeding)
behaviorNotes: Flash-frozen at peak ripeness. Often better nutrient retention than out-of-season fresh. Do not thaw for baking; fold in frozen. For sauces, thaw and use all juices.
limitations: Texture is mushy when thawed; not suitable for fresh garnish or fruit salads. Bleeds color into batter.

ratio: 1 medium shallot = 1/3 cup finely diced red onion
behaviorNotes: More pungent than shallot. Milder when cooked. Best in vinaigrettes (soak in acid 10 min to mellow). Good in salads and quick pickles.
limitations: Stronger onion flavor. Larger pieces; dice finely to approximate shallot texture. More pungent raw.

behaviorNotes: Similar acidity. Slightly different flavor profile (lime is more floral and tropical). Interchangeable in most cooking applications. Zest is not interchangeable as freely.
limitations: Different flavor character. Lime works better with Latin and Southeast Asian dishes; lemon with Mediterranean and French.

ratio: 1 tsp dried per 1 tbsp fresh (1:3 ratio)
behaviorNotes: Add dried herbs early in cooking (they need time to rehydrate and release flavor). Fresh herbs are best added at the end. Crush dried herbs between fingers before adding to release oils.
limitations: Some herbs do not dry well: basil, cilantro, parsley, chives, tarragon, dill lose significant flavor when dried. Oregano, thyme, rosemary, and sage dry well.

ratio: One 28oz can = about 2 lbs fresh tomatoes
behaviorNotes: Canned tomatoes are picked at peak ripeness. Often better than out-of-season fresh tomatoes. San Marzano or domestic equivalent for best quality. Crush by hand for chunky sauce.
limitations: Not suitable for fresh applications (salads, bruschetta). Different acidity profile than fresh.

ratio: 1:1 by weight
behaviorNotes: Blend until completely smooth. Works in cheesecakes, dips, and frostings. Add lemon juice for tanginess. Firm silken tofu blends best.
limitations: Contains soy. Less tangy than cream cheese. Different mouthfeel. Needs lemon juice and salt adjustment.

ratio: 1:1 (reduce other liquids by 2 tbsp per cup in baking)
behaviorNotes: Similar sweetness and viscosity. Different flavor (maple vs floral). Works in marinades, dressings, and baking. Grade A Dark has the strongest maple flavor for cooking.
limitations: Different flavor profile. Some vegans accept honey; confirm with client. Maple syrup is thinner than honey.

ratio: 1 tbsp soy sauce + 1 tsp balsamic + 1/2 tsp molasses per 1 tbsp Worcestershire
behaviorNotes: Traditional Worcestershire contains anchovies. This blend approximates the sweet-savory-umami profile. Adjust proportions to taste.
cuisineContext: Marinades, Caesar dressing, Bloody Mary, stews
limitations: Contains soy. Not identical flavor. Some commercial vegan Worcestershire sauces are available (Annie's brand).

ratio: 1 tsp agar powder per 1 tbsp gelatin powder (or 1 tsp per 4 sheets)
behaviorNotes: Sets firmer and at room temperature (no refrigeration needed). Must be boiled to activate (unlike gelatin which dissolves in warm liquid). Sets faster than gelatin.
limitations: Firmer, more brittle set (less jiggly). Does not melt in your mouth like gelatin. Cannot be remelted as easily. Acidic liquids weaken gel.

ratio: 1 tbsp lemon juice or vinegar + enough milk to make 1 cup (let stand 5-10 min)
behaviorNotes: The acid curdles the milk slightly, simulating buttermilk's acidity and thickness. Works in baking, pancakes, and fried chicken marinades. Use whole milk for best results.
limitations: Lacks the cultured flavor of true buttermilk. Thinner consistency. Acceptable for baking; less so for drinking or cold applications.

targetIngredient: gluten-free breadcrumbs or crushed rice cereal
behaviorNotes: GF panko is available (many brands). Crushed Rice Chex or cornflakes work as a coating. Toast for extra crunch.
limitations: Different texture. GF breadcrumbs may brown faster. Some brands contain soy.

behaviorNotes: Similar tanginess and texture. Higher protein, lower fat. Works in dips, baked potatoes, marinades, and baking. Full-fat yogurt is closest match.
limitations: Contains dairy (not suitable for dairy allergy). Slightly more tart than sour cream. May curdle at high temperatures.

behaviorNotes: Provides creaminess and fat. Adds green color and mild avocado flavor. Best in sandwiches, wraps, and as a spread. Add lime juice to prevent browning.
limitations: Browns when exposed to air. Adds distinct flavor. Does not work in baking recipes that call for mayo. Higher cost.

behaviorNotes: Thickens at lower temperature than cornstarch. Produces a glossy, clear sauce. Good for fruit sauces and glazes. Add at the end of cooking.
limitations: Breaks down with prolonged high heat. Does not work well in dairy-based sauces (produces slimy texture). More expensive than cornstarch.

targetIngredient: perilla oil or walnut oil + smoked paprika
ratio: 1:1 (walnut oil) + pinch smoked paprika for depth
behaviorNotes: No perfect substitute exists for toasted sesame oil's unique flavor. Walnut oil provides nuttiness; perilla oil is closest in Asian cooking. Use as finishing oil only.
limitations: Walnut oil contains tree nuts. Perilla oil may be hard to find. Neither perfectly replicates sesame flavor.

behaviorNotes: Similar consistency and fat content. Works in hummus, dressings, and baking. Slightly different flavor but functionally equivalent.
limitations: Different flavor profile. May turn green in baked goods with baking soda. Not sesame-flavored.

behaviorNotes: Similar size and appearance. Mild, nutty flavor. Do not toast as aggressively as sesame (burn easily). Good in salads, bowls, and as a garnish.
limitations: Will not replicate toasted sesame flavor. Softer texture. Higher cost.

behaviorNotes: Darker color, slight caramel/toffee flavor. Lower glycemic index than white sugar. Does not dissolve as easily in cold liquids. Works in baking and cooking.
limitations: Changes color of final product. More expensive than white sugar. FDA classifies coconut as tree nut for labeling.

behaviorNotes: Less fat than heavy cream but similar richness in cooked dishes. Does not whip. Good in soups, mac and cheese, and cream sauces.
limitations: Contains dairy. Cannot be whipped. Slightly cooked flavor. Thinner than heavy cream.

targetIngredient: chicken or vegetable broth + white wine vinegar
ratio: 3/4 cup broth + 1 tbsp white wine vinegar per 1 cup wine
behaviorNotes: Provides acidity and liquid volume. Missing the depth of wine. Add a squeeze of lemon for brightness. Works in pan sauces, deglazing, and risotto.
limitations: Does not replicate the complexity of wine reduction. Non-alcoholic wine is another option but varies in quality.

targetIngredient: coconut bacon (coconut flakes baked with soy sauce and smoked paprika)
ratio: 1:1 by volume as a topping
behaviorNotes: Smoky, salty, crispy when fresh. Bake coconut flakes with soy sauce, maple syrup, smoked paprika, and liquid smoke at 325F for 10-15 min. Stir frequently.
limitations: Does not render fat. No protein. Different texture when cooled (less crispy). Contains soy and coconut.

targetIngredient: crumbled firm tofu + nutritional yeast + lemon juice
ratio: 1:1 (14oz tofu + 2 tbsp nutritional yeast + 1 tbsp lemon juice per 15oz ricotta)
behaviorNotes: Crumble tofu, mix with nutritional yeast, lemon juice, salt, and Italian herbs. Works in lasagna, stuffed shells, and baked ziti. Drains well for stuffed pasta.
limitations: Contains soy. Different texture (grainier than ricotta). Less creamy. Needs seasoning.

behaviorNotes: Provides umami without fish. White miso is mildest. Works in Caesar dressing, pasta sauces, and anywhere anchovy provides background savoriness.
limitations: Contains soy. Different flavor profile. Miso adds saltiness; adjust other salt accordingly.

behaviorNotes: Caffeine-free. Naturally sweeter than chocolate, so reduce added sugar. Does not behave identically when melted. Dairy-free by default but check label.
limitations: Very different flavor. Most people expect chocolate and will notice the swap. Better as its own ingredient than as a substitute.

ratio: 1:1 (use 2 corn per 1 large flour for burritos/wraps)
behaviorNotes: Naturally gluten-free. Smaller and less pliable than flour tortillas. Warm before using (dry skillet 30 sec each side). Best for tacos, enchiladas, tostadas.
limitations: Tears easily when cold. Not suitable for large wraps or burritos without doubling up. Different flavor and texture.

behaviorNotes: Dark color and umami depth approximates beef broth. Use mixed dried mushrooms (porcini, shiitake) for complexity. Add soy sauce for extra depth.
limitations: Missing the gelatin body of bone broth. Different flavor character. Add a splash of soy for meatiness.

ratio: 1:1 by volume (cauliflower rice is much lower calorie)
behaviorNotes: Pulse raw cauliflower in food processor or buy pre-riced. Saute in oil 5-7 min; do not overcook. Season well. Works as a base for bowls and stir-fries.
limitations: Very different taste and texture. Releases water when cooking. Does not work for sushi, risotto, or fried rice.

ratio: 2 medium zucchini per 8oz pasta serving
behaviorNotes: Salt and drain for 15 minutes before cooking to remove excess water. Quick saute (2-3 min) or serve raw with warm sauce. Overcooking produces mush.
limitations: Very different texture. Releases water into sauce. Does not work with heavy cream sauces or baked pasta. Seasonal availability.

behaviorNotes: Closest body and protein content to soy milk among non-soy alternatives. Barista style froths well. Slightly sweet.
limitations: Contains gluten (oats may be cross-contaminated). Not safe for celiac unless certified GF oat milk.

behaviorNotes: Similar size, shape, and bright green color. Slightly different flavor (more earthy). Works in salads, bowls, and as a side.
limitations: Fava beans can trigger hemolytic reactions in people with G6PD deficiency (favism). Seasonal availability.

ratio: 1:1 by weight
behaviorNotes: Made from chickpea flour and water. Soy-free. Firmer than silken tofu. Pan-fries well. Can be made at home (chickpea flour + water, cook, chill, slice).
limitations: Different texture (denser). Less neutral flavor. Not widely available commercially; may need to make from scratch.

targetIngredient: gluten-free all-purpose flour blend (Bob's Red Mill 1-to-1, King Arthur Measure for Measure)
ratio: 1:1 (these blends are designed for direct substitution)
behaviorNotes: Pre-mixed blends include xanthan gum and starch ratios optimized for 1:1 swaps. Best all-around GF flour substitute. Results are very close to wheat in most recipes.
cuisineContext: All baking (cookies, cakes, muffins, pancakes, quick breads)
limitations: More expensive. Results vary by brand. Not ideal for yeast breads (use a bread-specific GF flour). Check for allergens (some contain soy).

behaviorNotes: Similar thickening power. Tolerates higher temperatures better than arrowroot. Clear finish. Good for gravies and sauces.
limitations: Breaks down with prolonged boiling. Different from potato flour (which is heavier and not interchangeable).

ratio: 1 tbsp garlic-infused oil + 1 tbsp chopped chives per 2 cloves garlic
behaviorNotes: FODMAPs are water-soluble but not fat-soluble, so garlic-infused oil provides garlic flavor without the FODMAPs. Chives add the allium visual. Works for FODMAP-sensitive clients.
limitations: Less intense garlic flavor. Must use oil-infused (not garlic pieces in oil). Homemade garlic oil has botulism risk; use commercially prepared or make fresh daily.

targetIngredient: green onion (green parts only) + asafoetida powder
ratio: 1/2 cup sliced green onion tops + 1/4 tsp asafoetida per 1 medium onion
behaviorNotes: Green parts of scallions are low-FODMAP. Asafoetida (hing) provides onion-like pungency. Bloom asafoetida in oil briefly before adding other ingredients.
limitations: Different flavor profile. Asafoetida is very pungent; use sparingly. Not a perfect match. Green onion whites are high-FODMAP.

ratio: 1:1 by volume (cooked)
behaviorNotes: Rinse quinoa before cooking to remove bitter saponins. Cook in 1.5:1 water ratio for 15 min. Fluff with fork. Similar grain-like texture but distinct nutty flavor.
cuisineContext: Salads, pilafs, grain bowls, side dishes
limitations: Different cook time and method. Couscous is faster (5 min). Quinoa has a distinct taste some find earthy.

ratio: 1:1 by volume
behaviorNotes: Drain, dry, toss with oil and salt, roast at 400F for 25-30 min until crunchy. Season with desired spices. Adds protein. Naturally gluten-free.
limitations: Different texture (crunchy but not bread-like). Lose crunch quickly in liquid. Legume allergy concerns.

behaviorNotes: Higher fiber and nutrition. Nuttier flavor and slightly chewier texture. Cooks 1-2 minutes longer than regular pasta. Works best with bold, robust sauces.
limitations: Still contains gluten. Different flavor that not all clients enjoy. Delicate cream sauces may be overpowered.

behaviorNotes: Very high smoke point (520F). Neutral flavor. Works for searing, roasting, and frying. More expensive but considered a healthier fat.
limitations: Higher cost. Some brands are adulterated (buy reputable brands). Mild avocado flavor is detectable in cold applications.

ratio: 1:1 by weight (adjust cooking method for protein type)
behaviorNotes: Alpha-gal syndrome is a tick-bite-induced allergy to mammalian meat (beef, pork, lamb). Poultry and fish are safe. Some patients also react to dairy and gelatin.
limitations: Cannot use any mammalian meat. Check if client also reacts to dairy or gelatin. Delayed reactions (3-6 hours) make diagnosis tricky.

behaviorNotes: Works well in sauces and soups. Does not whip. Slight oat flavor. Heat-stable for cooking. Available in most grocery stores.
limitations: Contains gluten (oat-based). Does not whip to peaks. Thinner than heavy cream.
